title: A First-Timer's Winter Sports & Snow Tour from Seoul: 2 Nights, 3 Days Itinerary
html:
If your trip to Korea lands sometime between mid-December and early March, you're visiting during the one stretch of the year when skiing, snowboarding, and ice skating are all easy to add to a Korea trip — even if you've never tried winter sports before and don't have a car. This itinerary mixes a day of city-based winter fun in Seoul with an overnight trip to a ski resort just outside the city, so you get both the snow-mountain experience and the easy, subway-and-bus version of winter in Korea.

This is a 2-night, 3-day plan: one day in Seoul, one full day (plus overnight) at a ski resort in Gangwon-do province, and a relaxed final morning back in the city before you head to your next stop. Nothing here requires prior ski experience — beginner lessons and rental gear are available everywhere you'll go.

Day 1: Ice Skating at Seoul Plaza


Seoul Plaza Ice Skating Rink, right in front of Seoul City Hall. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Ease into the winter theme with something you don't need to travel far for: the Seoul Plaza Ice Skating Rink, an outdoor rink set up every winter right in front of City Hall (subway Line 1 or 2, City Hall Station, Exit 5). It's an easy walk from Deoksugung Palace and the Seoul Metropolitan Library, so it's simple to combine with sightseeing earlier in the day.

The rink has separate areas for beginners and more confident skaters, with skate and helmet rental included in the admission price — in past seasons this has been as little as ₩1,000 for about an hour, which is one of the cheapest winter activities you'll find anywhere in the city. The rink usually opens in mid-to-late December and runs through early February, but exact opening dates shift slightly every year, so check the Seoul city tourism site or your hotel front desk for this winter's schedule before you go, especially if you're visiting in early December.

The rink stays open into the evening, with City Hall lit up behind it. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

If you've never skated before, don't worry — there are usually staff nearby to help first-timers get steady on their feet, and holding onto the side wall for your first few laps is completely normal, not embarrassing. Give yourself about an hour, which is typically how rental sessions are timed anyway.

💡 How locals actually do it: After skating, a lot of Koreans head straight to a jjimjilbang (a Korean bathhouse and sauna, usually open very late or 24 hours) to warm back up in the hot baths — it's the standard way to end a cold outdoor activity here. A simpler option on your way back to your hotel is grabbing a cup of hot sikhye (a sweet rice drink) or a warm hotteok (a filled pancake) from a street stall or convenience store — both are classic Korean ways to warm up outdoors in winter.

Day 2: Getting to Vivaldi Park Ski Resort


Vivaldi Park Ski World in Hongcheon, Gangwon-do — one of the closest full ski resorts to Seoul. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

In the morning, head out to Vivaldi Park Ski World in Hongcheon, Gangwon-do — about 1.5 hours from Seoul and one of the easiest ski resorts to reach without a car. The resort runs direct shuttle buses from several pickup points in Seoul (including spots near major subway stations), which you can usually book online or through a tour platform a few days ahead. A taxi or an intercity bus to Hongcheon followed by a local taxi also works, but the resort shuttle is by far the simplest option for first-timers.

Vivaldi Park has 12 slopes, one gondola, and 10 lifts, with runs for complete beginners all the way up to advanced skiers, so it's a reasonable choice whether this is your first time on snow or you've skied before back home. The condo-style accommodation at the resort has direct access to the slopes, which is worth booking for this trip so you're not wasting time traveling back and forth.

Check in to your resort accommodation first, drop your bags, and change into warm layers — you'll want a waterproof jacket and pants if you have them, or you can rent a full snow outfit at the resort if you're traveling light.

Day 2: Skiing and Snowboarding for Beginners


A wide beginner slope at Vivaldi Park, good for first-timers. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

If you've never skied or snowboarded before, book a beginner lesson at the resort's ski school rather than just renting gear and heading up alone — most resorts in Korea offer English-language group or private lessons, and a couple of hours with an instructor will save you a lot of falling and frustration. Full equipment rental (skis or snowboard, boots, helmet, poles) is available on-site, and lift tickets, lessons, and gear rental can usually be bundled together as a package, which tends to work out cheaper than booking each piece separately.

Beginner slopes are clearly marked (usually green), so stick to those for your first day. Once you're comfortable turning and stopping, the resort staff or your instructor can point you toward slightly steeper intermediate runs.

Vivaldi Park also offers night skiing, with the slopes lit up after dark. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Many Korean ski resorts, Vivaldi Park included, offer night skiing sessions on lit slopes, usually at a discounted rate compared to a full daytime pass — a fun option if you want to try skiing after dinner instead of doing a full day. If skiing isn't for you but you still want to be out in the snow, most Korean ski resorts also have a separate sledding or snow-tubing area that doesn't require any lessons at all.

💡 How locals actually do it: Korean skiers almost always end the day with a hot bowl of ramyeon (instant noodles) or eomuk (fish cake skewers in hot broth) from a snack stand right at the base of the slopes — it's less about the food itself and more about warming up fast after hours in the cold. Don't skip it just because it looks like a simple snack bar; it's part of the experience.

Exact resort opening dates for the season change slightly year to year (recent seasons have run roughly from early-to-mid December through late February or early March), so confirm this winter's dates and current lift ticket and lesson prices on the resort's official website before you book, since ski season pricing is updated yearly.

Day 3: A Slow Morning by the Han River Before You Head Back


Jamsil Hangang Park, one of several Han River parks in Seoul. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Take the morning shuttle or bus back to Seoul and ease into your last day rather than packing in more sightseeing. If you still have some snow energy left, several parks along the Han River (Hangang) — including Ttukseom Hangang Park, Jamwon Hangang Park, and Yeouido Hangang Park — set up free, temporary sledding hills for the public each winter, usually from late December into early February. These are run by the city, are either free or very cheap, and don't require any booking — just show up, though some locations give out a limited number of entry slots per day, so arriving earlier rather than later helps. Check the Hangang Park website or a Korean events app closer to your trip for which park is running sledding that winter, since the exact locations can shift slightly from year to year.

If sledding isn't running or isn't your thing, a relaxed walk along the frozen-looking riverside, a coffee at one of the park's cafés, or simply resting before your flight all work just as well for a final morning.

Here's how the ski resort options near Seoul compare, in case you want to adjust this itinerary:

ResortApprox. distance/time from SeoulGetting thereBest for
Vivaldi Park (Hongcheon)~1.5 hrsResort shuttle bus from Seoul, or intercity bus/taxiFirst-timers — most slopes and lifts, easiest shuttle booking
Elysian Gangchon (Chuncheon)~1–1.5 hrsITX-Cheongchun train to Gangchon Station, then a short shuttle — the only Korean ski resort reachable by trainTravelers without a car who prefer public transit over a bus shuttle
Jisan Forest Resort (Icheon)~1–1.5 hrsResort shuttle bus or private tour bus from Seoul (public transit is limited)Shorter day-trip skiing rather than an overnight stay

Since resort pickup points, shuttle schedules, and opening dates are updated for each new season, double-check the resort's official website or a current ski tour booking platform before you lock in your plans.

⛷️ Planning your first ski trip in Korea? Drop your questions in the comments below — happy to help you figure out the details!
meta_description: A beginner-friendly 2-night, 3-day Korea itinerary: Seoul ice skating, skiing at Vivaldi Park, and free Han River sledding.
